common_name: Angeleno Plum (Very Late-Season California Japanese Plum)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while dormant, in full sun with excellent drainage; needs a mid-season-blooming Japanese plum pollenizer nearby.

directions: Angeleno is a late-season Japanese plum developed in California and prized for extending the harvest into September, well after Santa Rosa and most other Japanese types have finished. The deep purple-black skin encloses meaty amber-yellow freestone flesh that holds up unusually well in storage and shipping compared to earlier-season Japanese plums. Because it blooms in mid-season, plant Angeleno with another mid-blooming Japanese plum such as Santa Rosa or Burgundy within about fifty feet to ensure a full crop. Thin fruit early to four to six inches apart so the remaining plums size up properly on this heavy-setting tree.

common_name: Black Amber Plum (Early-Season California Japanese Plum)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while dormant, in full sun with excellent drainage; requires a different mid-season Japanese plum pollenizer nearby.

directions: Black Amber (also sold as Blackamber) is an early-summer Japanese plum bred in California that has long been one of the most widely planted commercial plum varieties in the state. The nearly black skin covers firm amber flesh with a pleasant balance of sweetness and tartness, similar in appearance to the later-ripening Friar but ready weeks earlier in late June. The tree is vigorous and productive but needs a different mid-season-blooming Japanese plum nearby, such as Santa Rosa, for reliable pollination and fruit set. Its relatively low chilling requirement makes it a workable choice for warmer zone 8 and 9 gardens where many European plums fail to set fruit.

common_name: Nubiana Plum (Self-Fruitful Black-Skinned California Japanese Plum)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while dormant, in full sun with excellent drainage; fruit set and size improve with a second Japanese plum nearby even though the variety is largely self-fruitful.

directions: Nubiana is a California-bred Japanese plum valued for its large, firm, slightly flattened fruit with deep purplish-black skin and sweet amber flesh that has very little tartness even near the pit. It ripens in mid-to-late summer, generally a few weeks after Black Amber and ahead of late-season types like Angeleno, filling out the middle of the harvest calendar. Unlike many Japanese plums, Nubiana is usually described as self-fruitful, though fruit set and size typically improve with a second Japanese plum planted nearby. Its moderate chilling requirement makes it a reasonable candidate for milder zone 8 and warmer zone 9 orchards that still receive some winter chill.
sources: One Green World nursery variety description

common_name: Imperial Epineuse Plum (Historic French Prune-Type European Plum)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while dormant, in well-drained fertile soil in full sun; largely self-fertile but a nearby pollinator can improve set.

directions: Imperial Epineuse is a French heirloom European plum discovered near the Lot Valley prune-growing district of France and brought to American growers by a California nurseryman in 1883. It became a historic reference variety for prune flavor and is still grown for its rich, sweet flesh that dries into a prune without the lye-dip treatment many other plums require. The medium-to-large oval freestone fruit has thin skin mottled in red, purple, and yellow-green beneath a light natural bloom, and the firm, slightly fibrous flesh is juicy and full-flavored fresh or dried. As a European plum it blooms later than Japanese types, which improves frost avoidance, and it is generally self-fertile though a nearby pollinator can improve yields.

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; self-fruitful, so a single tree will bear a full crop.

directions: Patterson is a widely grown California canning apricot named for Patterson, California, long known as a self-proclaimed apricot capital. It became the standard commercial replacement for Blenheim in many orchards because of its reliable heavy bearing and firm, all-purpose fruit suited equally well to canning, drying, shipping, and fresh eating. The medium-sized, golden-orange freestone fruit ripens in mid-to-late June and the tree is self-fruitful, so a single tree will set a full crop without a pollinator. Patterson needs a moderate amount of winter chill, so it performs best in zone 6 through 9 gardens with a real, if mild, winter.

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; pair with Patterson, Castlebrite, or another overlapping-bloom apricot for reliable pollination.

directions: Robada is a California apricot bred from a cross of Orangered and a University of California breeding selection, prized for its striking bright red blush over golden-orange skin and deep orange, firm freestone flesh. It ripens very early, among the first apricots of the season in early June, and the firm flesh handles shipping better than many older early varieties. Robada is not reliably self-fruitful in most plantings, so pair it with Patterson, Castlebrite, or another apricot with overlapping bloom for a full crop. Its moderate chilling requirement suits zone 7 through 9 gardens that receive a real winter but still want an early, richly colored apricot.
